paper.title: Exposure to More Female Peers Widens the Gender Gap in STEM Participation
paper.code_data_availability: Information concerning access to the data used in this paper is available as supplemental material online. (p. 1010, author footnote)

registers.name_in_paper: Danish administrative data on high school students
annual data on educational enrollment and degree completion
registers.years: up to 20 years after high school entry
variables_mentioned: field, type and level of education (ISCED fields)
number of years after high school entry the individual was last observed

registers.name_in_paper: labor market data (annual earnings and occupation)
registers.years: up to 20 years after high school entry
variables_mentioned: occupation coded in the Danish version of the International Standard Classification of Occupations (DISCO)

registers.name_in_paper: administrative registries (parental background and family links)
variables_mentioned: mother's and father's highest educational degree and field of education
whether the child lives with both parents at age 10

linkages: administrative data on high school students linked to annual data on educational enrollment and degree completion
students linked to annual labor market data on earnings and occupation up to 20 years after high school entry
students linked to their mothers and fathers for parental education, field of education and family structure
students linked to their own children for the fertility outcomes

sample.universe: All first-year students enrolled in the math track of Danish general academic high schools from 1980 through 1994
sample.unit_of_observation: student (each individual represents one observation); the peer variable is defined at the school-by-cohort-by-track level and some auxiliary regressions (table 5) use the school cohort as the unit
selection_rules: exclude students with missing values for gender and age (0.8% of students)
exclude students who were not between 14 and 19 years old when entering the general high school (less than 0.01%)
restrict to schools in which at least 95% of students in a given cohort are 14-19 years old
exclude schools with cohort sizes of less than 10 students in a given year (these two restrictions exclude 6.1% of students)
restrict to schools that have been in existence and have admitted students for at least four consecutive years (excluding 0.6% of students)
sample.period: high school entry cohorts 1980-1994, followed up to 20 years after high school entry
sample.n_observations: 182,211 students in 127 schools and 1,877 school cohort observations

construction_notes: The proportion of female peers is constructed at the cohort-school-track level, excluding the individual himself or herself, and measured at the time of high school entry; students are on average exposed to 45% female peers and 1 SD equals 7.0 percentage points.

STEM is classified with the ISCED system: natural sciences, mathematics and statistics (ISCED-05), information and communication technologies (ISCED-06), and engineering, manufacturing and construction (ISCED-07).
STEM is split into four subfields: biology, math and physics, ICT and engineering, and manufacturing and construction.
Other fields considered: health sciences (ISCED-091), education (ISCED-01), arts/humanities (ISCED-02), social sciences (ISCED-031) and business/law (ISCED-04).
STEM completion uses the field of the highest obtained degree; enrollment variables are indicators for ever having been enrolled in the respective study at the college level or higher.

Working in STEM is an indicator for working in a high-skilled occupation within STEM (DISCO codes 21, 25, 31 or 35) for at least half the years observed, 11-15 and 16-20 years after high school entry respectively.

The earnings percentile is the average of the individual's labor earnings percentile during the 5-year period, calculated by year of birth and age using the entire Danish population as a reference group.
Annual labor earnings in table 1 are measured in thousand Danish kroner (1 USD = 6.6 DKK) and adjusted to 2015 prices.
High school GPA is standardized to mean 0 and standard deviation 1 and is observed only for students who completed general academic high school.
Standard errors are clustered at the school cohort level in the main models (tables 2 and 5 cluster at the school level).

links.pointer_quote: A 10 percentage point increase in the proportion of female high school peers lowers women's probability of enrolling in STEM studies by 1.4 percentage points, which is equivalent to a 6.4% decrease from the baseline.

claims.statement: A higher proportion of female high school peers reduces women's probability of enrolling in a STEM college program.

treatment.label: Proportion of female peers in the high school (math-track) cohort

definition.value: Share of female students in the individual's own high school cohort, constructed at the cohort-school-track level and excluding the individual himself or herself; measured at the time of high school entry. It enters equation (1) interacted with indicators for the student's own gender (Female_i and Male_i). Mean .45, 1 SD = 7.0 percentage points.

timing.value: measured at the time of high school entry (first year of the general academic high school math track)

outcome.label: STEM enrollment

definition.value: Indicator for whether the student enrolled in a STEM program in college within 20 years after high school entry; the enrollment variable is an indicator for the student's ever having been enrolled in the respective study at the college level or higher. STEM fields follow the International Standard Classification of Education (ISCED): natural sciences, mathematics and statistics (ISCED-05), information and communication technologies (ISCED-06), and engineering, manufacturing and construction (ISCED-07).

timing.value: within 20 years after high school entry

units.value: change in the probability of the 0/1 outcome indicator per one-unit (0 to 1) increase in the proportion of female peers; a 10 percentage point increase in the peer share corresponds to 0.1 times the coefficient

magnitude.interpretation: a 10 percentage point increase in the proportion of female high school peers lowers women's probability of enrolling in STEM by 1.4 percentage points, corresponding to a decrease of 6.4% relative to the baseline

estimand.time_horizon: within 20 years after high school entry
estimand.formal_query: E[Y | do(PropFemalePeers = p + 0.1), Female = 1] - E[Y | do(PropFemalePeers = p), Female = 1], for math-track high school entrants 1980-1994

population.description: First-year students in the math track of Danish general academic high schools, entry cohorts 1980-1994, after the sample restrictions of sec. II.B; 182,211 students in 127 schools and 1,877 school cohorts.
population.ages: 14-19 years old at high school entry
population.period: high school entry cohorts 1980-1994, followed up to 20 years after high school entry
population.selection: All first-year students in the general academic high school math track entering 1980-1994, after excluding students with missing gender or age (0.8%), students not aged 14-19 at entry (<0.01%), schools in which fewer than 95% of a cohort are 14-19 years old, schools with cohorts of fewer than 10 students (6.1%), and schools that had not admitted students for at least four consecutive years (0.6%).

identification.source_of_variation: Idiosyncratic year-to-year variation in the proportion of female students within Danish general academic high schools across entry cohorts 1980-1994, after taking out school fixed effects, cohort fixed effects and school-specific time trends.

key_assumptions.assumption: Year-to-year variation in the proportion of female students within a school is exogenous to factors affecting the outcome, conditional on school fixed effects, cohort fixed effects and school-specific time trends: no omitted variable exists that is time variant and school specific, not captured by school-specific time trends, correlated with both the peer composition and the outcome, and not included in the individual- and peer-level controls.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Balancing tests: own gender does not predict the female peer share (table 2); 190 bivariate regressions of background characteristics on the peer share (tables 3 and A1) yield shares of significant coefficients at or below chance; no school-level autocorrelation in the female share (table 4); no correlation between math- and language-track female shares (table 5); residualised variation closely follows the normal distribution (fig. 2).

key_assumptions.assumption: Students cannot anticipate or select on the realised gender composition of their high school track cohort: they apply in the winter of their last year of primary school and learn the composition only on the first day of high school, 6 months later.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Institutional description of the Danish high school application and admission timeline (sec. II.A).

key_assumptions.assumption: Admission committees did not consider the gender of applicants during the admission process.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Conversations with school principals active during the observation period (footnote 16).

key_assumptions.assumption: Student gender is observed in administrative registries and therefore measured without error, so the peer-share estimates are free from the upward bias classical measurement error can create in peer effects estimates.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argument in footnote 26, referring to Angrist (2014) and Feld and Zölitz (2017).

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference across school cohorts: a student's outcome depends on the gender composition of his or her own school-cohort peer group only, and not on the composition of other cohorts or schools.

threats_discussed: student sorting at various institutional levels: parents select into neighborhoods, students select into schools, and within schools students may select into classrooms or be assigned to tracks

mediators_claimed: gender gap in high school GPA (students' preparedness for STEM studies)

heterogeneity.finding: The influence of peers is twice as strong for women with parents without a college education (-.129, SE .028) as for women with college-educated parents (-.070, SE .030); effects for men do not vary by parental education (.091 vs .090). Table 9, cols. 3-4.

Women with a STEM-educated mother are not significantly affected (.077, SE .099), while the effect for women with a STEM father is similar to the full sample (-.115, SE .037); for men with a STEM father the effect is weaker and not significant (.045, SE .041). Table 9, cols. 5-6.

heterogeneity.dimension: number of high schools in the municipality
heterogeneity.finding: Point estimates for women are very similar in municipalities with only one high school (-.088, SE .030) and with two or more (-.097, SE .032); for men the effect is somewhat larger where there is only one high school (.107 vs .064). Table A3.
The test for gender equality of the proportion of female peers rejects equality of the female and male coefficients with p < .0001 (table 7, panel A).

given: gender gap in high school GPA (students' preparedness for STEM studies)

evidence.how: The regressor is the proportion of female peers measured on the 0-1 share scale, so the coefficient is the change in the outcome per one-unit change in that share; the paper reads its effects off as 0.1 times the coefficient for a 10 percentage point increase.
Read from the three asterisks printed on the coefficient and the table legend (* p < .1, ** p < .05, *** p < .01); the table prints no exact p-value for this coefficient.
Standard deviation of the outcome in the estimation sample, read from Table 1, panel A, 'Any STEM enrollment' (SD .407 for women, .485 for men).

value.as_printed: Y_isc = β1 Female_i × PropFemalePeers_isc + β2 Male_i × PropFemalePeers_isc + β3 Female_i + C_isc γ′ + e_isc
value.normalisation: Male_i is the omitted own-gender main effect (only Female_i enters on its own); the peer variable is a leave-out share on the 0-1 scale. C_isc collects the fixed effects, time trends and individual and peer controls that are added gradually.

value.claimed_domain: Denmark; the authors extend the finding to other environments only conditionally, 'to the extent that our results for Denmark replicate in other environments'.
boundary_conditions: the results are based on one country (Denmark)

anchor_quote.text: Overall, the estimates show that a higher proportion of female peers—independent of how we deﬁne the relevant group of peers—lowers women’s probability of enrolling in and graduating from STEM college programs, while the opposite is true …

claims.statement: A higher proportion of female peers in the math track raises me's probability of graduating with a college STEM degree.

treatment.label: Proportion of female peers in the high school (math-track) cohort

definition.value: Share of female students in the individual's own high school cohort, constructed at the cohort-school-track level and excluding the individual himself or herself; measured at the time of high school entry. It enters equation (1) interacted with indicators for the student's own gender (Female_i and Male_i). Mean .45, 1 SD = 7.0 percentage points.

timing.value: measured at the time of high school entry (first year of the general academic high school math track)

outcome.label: STEM degree completion

definition.value: Indicator for whether the student's highest completed education is at least at the college level and is within STEM. STEM fields follow the International Standard Classification of Education (ISCED): natural sciences, mathematics and statistics (ISCED-05), information and communication technologies (ISCED-06), and engineering, manufacturing and construction (ISCED-07).

timing.value: highest completed degree, observed over the 20 years after high school entry

units.value: change in the probability of the 0/1 outcome indicator per one-unit (0 to 1) increase in the proportion of female peers; a 10 percentage point increase in the peer share corresponds to 0.1 times the coefficient

estimand.time_horizon: highest completed degree, observed over the 20 years after high school entry
estimand.formal_query: E[Y | do(PropFemalePeers = p + 0.1), Male = 1] - E[Y | do(PropFemalePeers = p), Male = 1], for math-track high school entrants 1980-1994

population.description: First-year students in the math track of Danish general academic high schools, entry cohorts 1980-1994, after the sample restrictions of sec. II.B; 182,211 students in 127 schools and 1,877 school cohorts. Table 6 excludes the 727 students attending the 11 school cohorts without a language track, leaving 181,484 observations.
population.ages: 14-19 years old at high school entry
population.period: high school entry cohorts 1980-1994, followed up to 20 years after high school entry
population.selection: All first-year students in the general academic high school math track entering 1980-1994, after excluding students with missing gender or age (0.8%), students not aged 14-19 at entry (<0.01%), schools in which fewer than 95% of a cohort are 14-19 years old, schools with cohorts of fewer than 10 students (6.1%), and schools that had not admitted students for at least four consecutive years (0.6%).

identification.source_of_variation: Idiosyncratic year-to-year variation in the proportion of female students within Danish general academic high schools across entry cohorts 1980-1994, after taking out school fixed effects, cohort fixed effects and school-specific time trends.

key_assumptions.assumption: Year-to-year variation in the proportion of female students within a school is exogenous to factors affecting the outcome, conditional on school fixed effects, cohort fixed effects and school-specific time trends: no omitted variable exists that is time variant and school specific, not captured by school-specific time trends, correlated with both the peer composition and the outcome, and not included in the individual- and peer-level controls.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Balancing tests: own gender does not predict the female peer share (table 2); 190 bivariate regressions of background characteristics on the peer share (tables 3 and A1) yield shares of significant coefficients at or below chance; no school-level autocorrelation in the female share (table 4); no correlation between math- and language-track female shares (table 5); residualised variation closely follows the normal distribution (fig. 2).

key_assumptions.assumption: Students cannot anticipate or select on the realised gender composition of their high school track cohort: they apply in the winter of their last year of primary school and learn the composition only on the first day of high school, 6 months later.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Institutional description of the Danish high school application and admission timeline (sec. II.A).

key_assumptions.assumption: Admission committees did not consider the gender of applicants during the admission process.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Conversations with school principals active during the observation period (footnote 16).

key_assumptions.assumption: Student gender is observed in administrative registries and therefore measured without error, so the peer-share estimates are free from the upward bias classical measurement error can create in peer effects estimates.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argument in footnote 26, referring to Angrist (2014) and Feld and Zölitz (2017).

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference across school cohorts: a student's outcome depends on the gender composition of his or her own school-cohort peer group only, and not on the composition of other cohorts or schools.

anchor_quote.text: Overall, the estimates show that a higher proportion of female peers—independent of how we deﬁne the relevant group of peers—lowers women’s probability of enrolling in and graduating from STEM college programs, while the opposite is true …

claims.statement: A higher proportion of female peers in the math track raises me's probability of enrolling in a STEM college program.

treatment.label: Proportion of female peers in the high school (math-track) cohort

definition.value: Share of female students in the individual's own high school cohort, constructed at the cohort-school-track level and excluding the individual himself or herself; measured at the time of high school entry. It enters equation (1) interacted with indicators for the student's own gender (Female_i and Male_i). Mean .45, 1 SD = 7.0 percentage points.

timing.value: measured at the time of high school entry (first year of the general academic high school math track)

outcome.label: STEM enrollment

definition.value: Indicator for whether the student enrolled in a STEM program in college within 20 years after high school entry; the enrollment variable is an indicator for the student's ever having been enrolled in the respective study at the college level or higher. STEM fields follow the International Standard Classification of Education (ISCED): natural sciences, mathematics and statistics (ISCED-05), information and communication technologies (ISCED-06), and engineering, manufacturing and construction (ISCED-07).

timing.value: within 20 years after high school entry

units.value: change in the probability of the 0/1 outcome indicator per one-unit (0 to 1) increase in the proportion of female peers; a 10 percentage point increase in the peer share corresponds to 0.1 times the coefficient

estimand.time_horizon: within 20 years after high school entry
estimand.formal_query: E[Y | do(PropFemalePeers = p + 0.1), Male = 1] - E[Y | do(PropFemalePeers = p), Male = 1], for math-track high school entrants 1980-1994

population.description: First-year students in the math track of Danish general academic high schools, entry cohorts 1980-1994, after the sample restrictions of sec. II.B; 182,211 students in 127 schools and 1,877 school cohorts. Table 6 excludes the 727 students attending the 11 school cohorts without a language track, leaving 181,484 observations.
population.ages: 14-19 years old at high school entry
population.period: high school entry cohorts 1980-1994, followed up to 20 years after high school entry
population.selection: All first-year students in the general academic high school math track entering 1980-1994, after excluding students with missing gender or age (0.8%), students not aged 14-19 at entry (<0.01%), schools in which fewer than 95% of a cohort are 14-19 years old, schools with cohorts of fewer than 10 students (6.1%), and schools that had not admitted students for at least four consecutive years (0.6%).

identification.source_of_variation: Idiosyncratic year-to-year variation in the proportion of female students within Danish general academic high schools across entry cohorts 1980-1994, after taking out school fixed effects, cohort fixed effects and school-specific time trends.

key_assumptions.assumption: Year-to-year variation in the proportion of female students within a school is exogenous to factors affecting the outcome, conditional on school fixed effects, cohort fixed effects and school-specific time trends: no omitted variable exists that is time variant and school specific, not captured by school-specific time trends, correlated with both the peer composition and the outcome, and not included in the individual- and peer-level controls.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Balancing tests: own gender does not predict the female peer share (table 2); 190 bivariate regressions of background characteristics on the peer share (tables 3 and A1) yield shares of significant coefficients at or below chance; no school-level autocorrelation in the female share (table 4); no correlation between math- and language-track female shares (table 5); residualised variation closely follows the normal distribution (fig. 2).

key_assumptions.assumption: Students cannot anticipate or select on the realised gender composition of their high school track cohort: they apply in the winter of their last year of primary school and learn the composition only on the first day of high school, 6 months later.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Institutional description of the Danish high school application and admission timeline (sec. II.A).

key_assumptions.assumption: Admission committees did not consider the gender of applicants during the admission process.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Conversations with school principals active during the observation period (footnote 16).

key_assumptions.assumption: Student gender is observed in administrative registries and therefore measured without error, so the peer-share estimates are free from the upward bias classical measurement error can create in peer effects estimates.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argument in footnote 26, referring to Angrist (2014) and Feld and Zölitz (2017).

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference across school cohorts: a student's outcome depends on the gender composition of his or her own school-cohort peer group only, and not on the composition of other cohorts or schools.

treatment.label: Proportion of female peers in the high school (math-track) cohort

definition.value: Share of female students in the individual's own high school cohort, constructed at the cohort-school-track level and excluding the individual himself or herself; measured at the time of high school entry. timing.value: measured at the time of high school entry (first year of the general academic high school math track)

outcome.label: STEM degree completion

definition.value: Indicator for whether the student's highest completed education is at least at the college level and is within STEM. claims.statement: A higher proportion of female high school peers raises men's standardized high school GPA.

treatment.label: Proportion of female peers in the high school (math-track) cohort

definition.value: Share of female students in the individual's own high school cohort, constructed at the cohort-school-track level and excluding the individual himself or herself; measured at the time of high school entry. units.value: standard deviations of high school GPA per one-unit (0 to 1) increase in the proportion of female peers

identification.source_of_variation: Idiosyncratic year-to-year variation in the proportion of female students within Danish general academic high schools across entry cohorts 1980-1994, after taking out school fixed effects, cohort fixed effects and school-specific time trends.

key_assumptions.assumption: Year-to-year variation in the proportion of female students within a school is exogenous to factors affecting the outcome, conditional on school fixed effects, cohort fixed effects and school-specific time trends: no omitted variable exists that is time variant and school specific, not captured by school-specific time trends, correlated with both the peer composition and the outcome, and not included in the individual- and peer-level controls.

key_assumptions.assumption: Students cannot anticipate or select on the realised gender composition of their high school track cohort: they apply in the winter of their last year of primary school and learn the composition only on the first day of high school, 6 months later.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Institutional description of the Danish high school application and admission timeline (sec. II.A).

key_assumptions.assumption: Admission committees did not consider the gender of applicants during the admission process.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Conversations with school principals active during the observation period (footnote 16).

key_assumptions.assumption: Student gender is observed in administrative registries and therefore measured without error, so the peer-share estimates are free from the upward bias classical measurement error can create in peer effects estimates.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argument in footnote 26, referring to Angrist (2014) and Feld and Zölitz (2017).

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference across school cohorts: a student's outcome depends on the gender composition of his or her own school-cohort peer group only, and not on the composition of other cohorts or schools.
